captions: Chapter five. The small-cap hunter.

Not every winner concentrates. Our next investor
does the

opposite — dozens of small, careful bets, letting
the
winners carry the pack.

Ashish Kacholia is one of India's most respected
small-cap
specialists.

His disclosed portfolio spans roughly forty-eight
companies — a

deliberately wide net across engineering, pharma,
and niche manufacturing.
And it worked, hard, this year: his disclosed book

jumped about forty-seven percent in a single quarter
—
from around two thousand two hundred crore in March
to over three thousand two hundred crore by June.

His largest bet, Shaily Engineering Plastics, is
worth over
seven hundred crore.
The philosophy is simple to say and brutally hard
to do.

Find small companies before the crowd. Do the
homework
nobody else will. Size each position so a single
mistake can't sink you.
Then let the two or three that truly work
compound into the bulk of your returns.

It's the venture-capital mindset, applied to listed
small-caps —
and you've never heard of most of his names.
That's exactly the point. He's early, not loud.
Here's something important.

Damani won by owning essentially one stock. Kacholia
won
by owning nearly fifty.
So which is correct?
Both.

Concentration and diversification are just two
honest answers to
risk. What they share is the discipline behind every
single position — and the patience to hold it.
That's the constant.
